linkedin_activity.text: In a room full of social entrepreneurs at World Economic Forum 90% raised their hand when asked if they were concerned about the current state of AI today… After being immersed in this space for the last 9 months and talking to hundreds of CHWs, NGO staff, government officials and technologists with the team at Community Health Impact Coalition , I’m not surprised . Some quick (and non exhaustive) thoughts on why the feeling was probably so unanimous based on these conversations: 1. Lack of autonomy and say in how tools are deployed - only 15% of CHWs are involved in co-design of AI solutions. 2. The field moving faster than our ability to understand the latest developments, with no time to reflect individually or collectively on the question “is this what we really want for ourselves and our communities?” 3. Tools being deployed without rigorous / useful evaluation. 4. A lack of honest, simple public-facing communication so that people have a sense of what actually tools do and how they work. As a general rule of thumb people don’t trust things they don’t understand. 5. A breakdown in human-human interaction which can erode community connectedness and knowledge. 6. Extractive patterns being deployed across the space. But there was a positive emerging from the meeting… We discussed how a coalition approach to AI deployment could be the way forward. Working for CHIC and seeing the power of collective action to try solve big goals on a daily basis, I am slightly biased. But a high trust group working towards a shared commitment to common good resource mobilisation, knowledge sharing, and honest evaluation is critical at this time. Both to foster a sense of community but also to develop deep shared knowledge, avoid duplication and collectively figure out where all of this is going… Looking forward to taking this work forward in the community health space with all of the team involved in this. Huge thanks to Daniel Nowack , Sophia Otoo and the team at Schwab Foundation for Social Entrepreneurship for convening such a great meeting. Super work. ...more

5 reflections one week on from the Community Health AI workshop at Skoll: Last week, 80 individuals - including CHWs, technologists from Anthropic and Google.org , NGO implementers, funders - gathered for a workshop Community Health Impact Coalition convened alongside the Skoll World Forum. Just getting these groups in the same room - to work through what AI should (and shouldn't) do for the millions of CHWs serving as the front door to healthcare for hundreds of millions of people - felt like a success. Key take homes: 𝟭. 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿. The most consistent diagnosis of why AI tools fail CHWs? The absence of meaningful co-design. Tools designed in places where the end users do not work or live. 💡 Amref Health Africa 's CHA Reporting Assistant in Machakos - built via WhatsApp using a Problem-Alignment-Co-design-Evidence framework - is one of the counter-examples worth knowing about (cc: Aloise Gikunda ) 𝟮. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲. We heard from IDinsight and Last Mile Health that 91% of health extension workers using their HEP Assist tool in Ethiopia named poor connectivity as their primary barrier. 💡 As Emilie Chambert put it (and I will use this quote a lot in the coming months...!) "You can't AI your way out of a broken system." 𝟯. 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝘂𝗽. 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 𝗿𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸. A great quote from one group: "CHWs are net producers of data and net consumers of nothing." 💡 AMREF's work in Kenya - surfacing new health patterns in 76% of cases and feeding insights back to community health units - shows what closing that loop actually looks like. 𝟰. 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲. The point isn't to turn frontline decision-makers into data-entry clerks. 💡 Audere 's CHW companion - built explicitly for the worker, not the patient, and grounded in local context, language and guidelines - is one model. Generic LLMs do OK; but specific AI solutions built with context in mind are also really important. 𝟱. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘂𝗲 𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸. This was the second time in 12 months CHIC has convened funders, technologists and implementers to wrestle with tech, data and AI in the community health space - and the community is better for it. 💡 Solving this separately is how we got here. Solving it together is how we get out. Whether AI strengthens the global CHW workforce or quietly displaces it is one of the most consequential design choices global health will make this decade. ▶️ If you want to be part of this group and help address it, please reach out. A huge thanks to everyone who showed up, for the rich discussions and collaborative spirit, and to the partners we co-designed this with: IDinsight , Last Mile Health , Mozilla Data Collective , DataKind , Living Goods , Medic , Audere . ...more

The AI research I lead alongside a team of 50+ collaborators at Community Health Impact Coalition has been shortlisted for the 2026 The Elsevier Foundation - The Lancet Group Evidence to Impact Awards. Our submission "Artificial Intelligence in Community Healthcare: A Coalition Approach to Building the Evidence, Governance, and Implementation Architecture for Ethical AI in Community Health Systems," reflects months of work across the coalition to articulate what responsible AI in community health systems actually requires - and how a coalition can build the evidence base, governance, and implementation scaffolding to get there. A huge thanks to the entire team involved in this application, and to the Elsevier Foundation and The Lancet for the recognition. For those interested in where our work is heading, check out our latest piece on AI governance published in The Lancet Primary Care: https://lnkd.in/eaQhq_pR Full award shortlist here: https://lnkd.in/eax23X9Y ...more

3 reflections from an incredible week at Skoll World Forum 2026… 1. AI in global health is moving fast - radical collaboration is the answer. I went to 7 workshops on AI in global health and social innovation (...and could have gone to 7 more). The space is moving at such speed that we risk jumping on the hype train without knowing the final destination - and missing important stops along the way. What's needed are tight, high-trust spaces where organisations can share lessons, build joint datasets, and wrestle with the neglected questions: data ownership, community involvement in designing AI tools, and moving past the obsession with diagnostics toward the "boring but essential" work of governance, frameworks, and the tools that help with health systems strengthening. As Emilie Chambert put it: "You can't AI your way out of a broken system." Our "sold out" workshop on AI in the CHW space had 100+ people with standing room only. The appetite for shared learning is clearly there. Now let’s build on it so we're not back in 12 months having the same conversations. 2. Get out of your bubble. Day to day, my work is pretty focussed. That matters if you're going to move the needle. You can't be everything to everyone. But it pays to step outside your lane and listen to what others are doing. Shannon Farley ’s quote was one of the best: "The organisations that get this right aren't the ones who move fastest - they're the ones who know exactly what they don't know." Knowing what you don't know means being open to learning from spaces outside your own. Two things I took away from other sectors: - Digital Green … their AI-powered assistant reaches 250,000+ farmers and extension workers across India, Kenya, Nigeria and Ethiopia supporting low-literacy users in local languages, with trust and context as the hard problems. A lot to learn here. Manu Chopra and his team at Karya have built what they call "the world's first ethical data company," paying rural Indian workers $5/hour (roughly 20x the minimum wage) to generate AI training data in underrepresented Indian languages. Workers also receive royalties when their datasets are resold. A model challenging the status quo for who captures the value AI creates. We know we need to pay CHWs a salary - now we need to think seriously about how they and their communities are compensated for the data they generate. 3. AI can't replace human connection. The week was packed with AI-focused workshops, talks, and seminars but the most powerful part for me was meeting old and new friends face to face…some of the brightest and best people I know. That gave me huge renewed energy and new ideas. It also reminded me we're all wrestling with the same challenges and we’re all trying our best to figure it out. It’s better to do that together. If you'd like to join us at Community Health Impact Coalition as we continue building a community in the global community health AI space, reach out. ...more

As our 2025 Annual Report has gone live this week, I've been thinking about what made 2025 feel meaningful at Community Health Impact Coalition despite everything going on in the global climate. And honestly - I kept coming back to the people in these photos. None of us will pretend it was an easy year. Funding cuts, political uncertainty, brilliant friends and colleagues losing jobs, CHWs messaging with stories of stockouts and payment freezes. The anxiety was - and is - real. But this team still showed up. Because we know that administrations will come and go; but the communities who depend on CHWs for vital, lifesaving care at the last mile remain. That's not going to change. So neither can we. Given this, I am super proud to share the 2025 CHIC Annual Report. This includes the work of the Research Tactic I lead - and of every collaborator, ally, and partner who made this year's progress possible. 💡 One of the biggest outputs from our team last year was the most comprehensive analysis of CHW programme costs and cost-effectiveness in LMICs ever published - 6 papers across The Lancet Primary Care, BMJ Global Health, and PLOS Global Health, involving 30+ collaborators including CHWs, spanning sub-Saharan Africa, South and South East Asia, the US, and Latin America. But here's what I want to stress most: we were just as intentional about getting that evidence into the right hands as we were about producing it. High-quality research that sits in a journal changes nothing. So alongside publication we: ▶️ Designed evidence briefs delivered directly to Ministers of Health working hand in hand with our Policy and Advocacy colleagues to make sure the evidence landed where decisions are made. ▶️ Launched an innovative video podcast series on the use of data in CHW programmes, bringing together 18 guests from across the field produced over 2 days in London with SomX . ▶️ Convened 35+ collaborators for an in-person workshop and kicked off a 50-person collaboration on AI in CHW programmes - presenting to funders including the Gates Foundation to help guide investments through collective wisdom. ▶️ Provided GAVI and the Global Fund with economic evidence to strengthen proCHW decision-making processes. In a year defined by division, our team came together, looked out for each other, and delivered. And that matters just as much as anything we published. Read the full report and everything achieved by the Coalition in 2025 here: https://lnkd.in/eGG4nT9x ...more

Delighted to see our team’s latest article on governance of AI solutions in Community Health Worker (CHW) programmes published in The Lancet Primary Care . This paper showcases the amazing collaborative effort which lies at the heart of Community Health Impact Coalition . We brought together nearly 50 partners across more than a dozen countries, including funders, CHWs, government leaders, NGOs, and technical partners to write this piece...every author provided significant and unique contributions and I am really proud of our team's final piece. At its core, the message is simple but urgent: “The real danger is not failure, but scaling on terms that undermine care, trust, and professional judgement.” 📍 AI in community health is not a technology challenge - it’s a systems challenge. Without public stewardship, shared learning, and workforce readiness, we risk repeating the fragmentation of previous digital health waves. But done right, the opportunity is enormous - to strengthen (not replace) one of the world’s largest frontline workforces, and to translate AI into real gains in equity and access. This work is directly shaping the next phase of our efforts… Later this month, we’ll be convening a workshop during Skoll World Forum - bringing together frontier AI labs, funders, governments, NGOs, and CHWs to align on how we move from pilots to integrated, scalable systems. Exciting times for the CHW–AI space - and proud that all of our members and allies at Community Health Impact Coalition are helping to convene and drive this agenda forward in a truly collaborative fashion. #AI #GlobalHealth #CommunityHealth #HealthSystems #DigitalHealth ...more

Millions of people now turn to AI chatbots when they are struggling. Today in Nature Medicine ( Nature Portfolio ) we publish #SIMVAIL , an automated framework for evaluating #AI #chatbot safety in mental-health contexts. 🧠 Studying these interactions with real users raises obvious ethical problems, so we leveraged recent advances in LLM-based adversarial red-teaming, powered by Petri, Anthropic 's open-source auditing framework, to simulate clinically realistic multi-turn conversations at scale. #SIMVAIL simulates users with specific psychological vulnerabilities (depression, mania, psychosis, OCD, insecure attachment) and conversational intentions. It then scores every turn across clinical risk dimensions, with automated ratings validated against clinician judgement. Across 810 conversations with nine frontier models and >90,000 clinical ratings, we found that risk accumulated over turns, and varied depending on user vulnerability. We found a recurrent pattern driving risk, which we term a Vulnerability-Amplifying Interaction Loop (VAIL): cases where chatbot behaviours that are broadly supportive, such as validation, become maladaptive when they align with the mechanisms sustaining a user's vulnerability. Our results also point to some encouraging trends. First, newer models were safer. Second, replacing a single concerning response early in an interaction led to safer subsequent exchanges, suggesting that targeted intervention at points of escalation can change the trajectory of an entire conversation. 📈 We believe methods like #SIMVAIL address a gap in conversational AI safety evaluation in mental-health contexts. They allow us to localise when and where a model becomes unsafe, and then to test whether a proposed safeguard addresses the issue before launch. We've released the full dataset through the open #SIMVAIL Explorer, to encourage adoption by the wider community 📊 Led by Veith Weilnhammer ( UCL ), supported by Kevin Hou ( University of Sydney ), Lennart Luettgau & Chris Summerfield ( AI Security Institute (AISI) ) and Ray Dolan (UCL). This work would not have been possible without support from an AI Security Institute (AISI) Challenge Fund Award 🙏 University of Oxford , University of Oxford, Department of Psychiatry , UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology , Microsoft AI

Learning, learning, and more learning: 🔹 Learning from my "living group": Deeply grateful for the candid advice, strategic pressure-testing, and camaraderie from peer leaders like Margarita Guzman , Jill Sundstrom , Adav Noti , Rachel Kingston , James Evans , Amy McCreath, and Andreas Karelas . 🔹 Learning from HBS Faculty: Incredible gratitude to HBS Social Enterprise Initiative and Brian Trelstad , Shawn Cole , Monique Burns Thompson , John J-H Kim , Archie L. For those who've spent time in global health market shaping: this will feel familiar. Markets fail the people who need them most when there's no visibility into demand, no incentive to invest, and no one correcting for who's been left out. The same logic applies to medical innovations built on AI. A diagnostic tool or clinical assistant trained without exposure to how care is actually delivered in will underperform exactly where need is greatest. Closing the data gap is now as much a market shaping problem as lowering prices. I'm excited that we now have a place that puts communities at the centre of this challenge to build products that work for everyone, where they set the terms for how their data is used, and where they share in the value it generates.

I've spent much of my career working at the intersection of innovation, evidence, and implementation. One question keeps coming up: How do we ensure that research actually leads to better outcomes for children? That's why I'm excited to share our new paper, published in the JoGH World , examining UNICEF-supported embedded implementation research initiatives across multiple countries. The findings reinforce something that sounds like common sense, but is not yet standard practice: evidence is far more likely to drive change when research is conducted with decision-makers rather than for them. Across the projects analysed, embedded implementation research contributed to policy adaptations, programme improvements, and stronger service delivery, particularly in areas such as immunisation and child health. As global health systems face increasingly complex challenges, we need approaches that help us learn and adapt in real time. Embedded implementation research is one way of closing the gap between knowing and doing. Grateful to my co-authors and colleagues across countries who contributed to this work. ASM Shahabuddin, PhD Robert Scherpbier Alyssa Beth Sharkey 🔗 https://lnkd.in/dQrBudNi #ImplementationResearch #GlobalHealth #LearningHealthSystems #UNICEF #HealthInnovation

In a new Expert Comment piece written for the University of Oxford , ‘Who gets to define care in the age of AI?’, Dr Caroline Emmer De Albuquerque Green , Director of Research and Head of Public Engagement at the Institute for Ethics in AI , examines the growing use of the language of care by AI companies. She argues that the future of AI in social care must be shaped in genuine partnership with the care community, ensuring that those who provide and receive care have a meaningful role in defining how these technologies are developed and used. 📄 Read the full Expert Comment piece: https://lnkd.in/e2i4naVP

As Ebola transmission was exploding in West Africa in late 2014, Devabhaktuni Srikrishna , Jeffrey Sachs, and I published a paper in the Lancet, outlining a systematic approach to getting R below 1. That article led to a meeting with Guinea’s president and senior leadership. They asked me to come to Conakry for a week to see whether what needed to happen was getting done. That week turned into a year and a half. Over that time, working alongside Jean-Vivien MOMBOULI and other colleagues, we helped build a national response. The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak now unfolding in eastern DRC is at a similar inflection point, but under even harder conditions of conflict, displacement, fragmented authority, and deep distrust. In Council on Foreign Relations 's Think Global Health, Jean-Vivien and I reflect on our experiences from Guinea and consider what it will take to turn the tide in eastern DRC. The tools for controlling Ebola are known. The hard part is making them work together across many organizations and local outbreaks, while continually closing operational gaps, negotiating access, and earning community trust. https://lnkd.in/gzGwBxfM

Compensated Datasets is now live. 🎉 Today, we're making our first Compensated Datasets available through Mozilla Data Collective. Whether you're building AI applications, training models or looking for responsibly sourced data for your next project, Compensated Datasets makes it easier to discover and license multilingual, multicultural and multimodal datasets that are thoughtfully documented, transparently licensed and created by organisations and communities around the world. At the same time, data providers retain control over pricing and licensing terms, helping advance a more transparent and sustainable approach to data sharing grounded in human agency and fair value exchange. We're excited to launch with a series of unique global community datasets. Our amazing early partners include TAUS , Pangeanic , Karya , Spotlite and ContentX Labs , with more providers announcing in the coming weeks! 👉 Browse available datasets: https://lnkd.in/dzTad4_V #MozillaDataCollective #DataRights #FairData #Datasets

I'm excited to share that our research paper, "Machine Learning Analysis of Maternal Mortality Determinants in Nigeria: An Exploratory Study," has been published in The International Journal of Health Planning and Management. Working on this project gave me the opportunity to learn how data and machine learning can be used to better understand complex global health challenges. It also reinforced something I've come to believe through my work with Sim4Impact-innovation in healthcare isn't just about new technology. It's about asking better questions, collaborating across disciplines, and finding ways to improve patient outcomes. I'm incredibly grateful to my mentor Dr Abimbola Olaniran MD, PhD, NCA-Gen AI LLM, EMBA, P.M.P , co-authors and mentors for trusting me with the opportunity to contribute to this work. As a high school student interested in medicine, this experience has strengthened my passion for combining research, technology, and medical education to improve healthcare. https://lnkd.in/gk2egymw #Research #GlobalHealth #MachineLearning #MedicalResearch #MaternalHealth #HealthcareInnovation #StudentResearch #Sim4Health #sim4impact
